line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Be7
teaches: Against a gambit you do not have to meet sharpness with sharpness — a modest retreat that pre-answers the standard attacking idea is a complete strategy. Slightly passive and completely solid beats theoretical and half-remembered, especially when the attacker is counting on you to know less than they do.
explains: The bishop drops back to e7, and the knight's leap to g5 — the move every attack in this structure begins with — now lands on a square the bishop already covers. The retreat looks like a concession and is actually a preparation: the attack's first move has been answered before it was played.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4 Bc5 c3 Be7 Qc2 Na5 Qb3 d3
teaches: An extra gambit pawn is a bargaining chip, and sometimes its best move is to give itself back on the most annoying square available — pushed into the heart of their queenside, it sits on the squares their pieces need to develop through, so they spend moves removing it and you spend those moves developing.
explains: The pawn has advanced to d3, where it takes both c2 and e2 in hand — the queen's home diagonal square and the king's bishop's only developing square. Until it is dealt with, the pieces behind those squares are staring at a wall the opponent has to spend real moves dismantling.
